title: Part II — Some Political & Historical Context
paragraphs: The second half of the book opens with a scene that crystallizes its puzzle. Volunteering at NOSA in San Francisco in 1998, Gershon watches a meeting between Tim, a representative of the city's Department of Human Services, and three rival Samoan organizations. Fresh from New Zealand — where talk of cultural difference was constant — she expects the conversation to be about cultural sensitivity. Instead Tim proposes a scheme of "governmentally engineered extended families" to meet welfare-to-work deadlines, and never mentions culture at all.

The turning point comes when Gershon finally asks whether families would be matched with attention to cultural background. Tim's answer is a flat "no, absolutely not": placements must use race-blind criteria to guarantee equal treatment. She asked about culture; he answered about race. Then Michael, director of the Samoan Community Development Center, says he is tired of all the culture talk and just wants "competent families." In the US, Gershon realizes, a family can be classified as cultural or as merely competent — and competence trumps culture.

This sets up the comparison that drives Chapters 3–5. During her fieldwork both countries were absorbing sweeping neoliberal welfare reforms — New Zealand's 1989 CYPF Act and the US Personal Responsibility Act of 1996. Governments everywhere were rethinking their obligations to families. Yet Samoan migrants responded very differently in each place, and the key variable was how, and when, differences were made cultural.

Here Gershon introduces the concept that organizes the rest of the book: reflexivity, and specifically a clash of reflexivities. She flags that she uses "reflexivity" in the linguistic-anthropological sense — a contextually specific awareness of how self, others, and agency are related within a social order — not the familiar sense of an ethnographer reflecting on her own biases. Different social orders demand different reflexivities, and Part II examines what happens when Samoan culture-bearers meet officials whose reflexivity is entirely different.

The bulk of the chapter is a comparative history of governmental multiculturalism. Since the 1970s, each country's definition of "relevant difference" was forged in negotiation with its dominant minorities — Māori in New Zealand; African Americans, Hispanics, and Asian Americans in the US. Samoans are a minor minority in both, so they inherit categories built for others. In New Zealand, because Māori are Polynesian and understood as culture-bearers, Samoans get bracketed with them and benefit: the Treaty of Waitangi framework made culture a fundable treasure, and Samoans could claim parallel funding for scholarships and language programs.

In the US, by contrast, Samoans are located through census categories (long lumped under "Asian/Pacific Islander," too diverse to anchor any single fundable culture) and racialized along a race-and-class axis. The American parallel to New Zealand's "cultural expert" is merely a "minority expert." Because the major US minorities do not foreground culture in the New Zealand way, Samoan techniques for articulating cultural distinctiveness fall on deaf ears. Add the church-state divide (which blocks funding through Samoan churches) and diaspora's erosion of the chiefly system, and US Samoan organizations — often run by women, rarely by chiefs — are left doubly exposed. That is the setup for Chapter 3.
